design_notes: The error handling here is intentionally minimal by design: retries and alerting belong to the batch caller, not this layer. If a DELETE fails for a particular id, the best behavior for a sweep across a few hundred resources is to continue and report exactly what succeeded—killing the entire run over one transient connection hiccup throws away all the work already completed. The returned list hands the orchestrator a precise diff to guide the next pass, and because deletes are idempotent, re-running against whatever ids were missed converges naturally with no special handling needed. At this layer, timeouts and connection errors are the realistic transient failure modes; anything more fundamental (auth problems, 5xx responses) will show up in the orchestrator's own monitoring via the run's completion ratio. Adding raise_for_status to each request would simply transform a single bad id into a crashed sweep, and implementing local retry logic around each call would duplicate what the caller already handles on its schedule. Keeping the success path linear also makes the final completion report straightforward to reason about.

On how I approached the tests: I intentionally stayed away from golden-style assertions on exact values. For a validator, the contract that matters is structural — records split into two buckets, invalid entries include their index, the original record, and a list of errors, and together `valid + invalid` must account for everything that went in. If we asserted on precise error messages, every rewording would break the suite; and pinning exact bucket contents would fall apart as soon as someone tightened, say, the email rule. So these tests lock down the contract, not how it's implemented.

The type-level assertions are there to catch the regressions that show up in real life: a function returning `None` instead of a tuple, the invalid-entry shape getting flattened, or the index going missing. The identity comparison in the final test is the invariant I care most about — the record that comes back has to be the same object that went in, because downstream callers frequently feed it into correction workflows. Invariants written in a property-testing style (the partition is complete, positions are preserved) hold up much better over time than golden values, and they give quick feedback while you're iterating on the validator itself.

Some comments on how errors are handled, since that's the aspect most likely to attract scrutiny.

The insert loop fails soft on purpose. Logs are written by many producers, and any given line might hit a rotation race or show up truncated; killing the entire run because of one problematic line would leave ingest worse off than if we'd simply skipped it. SQLite lock contention is transient by its nature, so quietly eating the occasional per-row `OperationalError` and letting the next scheduled run re-read that section costs less than a retry loop that repeats work the scheduler already performs.

As for the offset: I store the file size rather than a per-row checkpoint because the ingest is idempotent at the run level — an interrupted run leaves the offset untouched, and the following run converges by re-processing. Alerting and retries belong to the caller, so wiring up local success/failure machinery here would only add redundant chatter between two components that already have it. Keeping the happy path linear also makes the resume behavior — seek, iterate, persist — trivially auditable at a glance, which I'd contend counts for more than defensive branches that trigger a few times a year.

The error handling in this layer is intentionally minimal, on the principle that retries and alerting belong to the batch caller. If a DELETE for a single id fails during a sweep across a few hundred resources, the right behavior is to continue through the rest and report which ones succeeded—killing the entire run because of one transient connection hiccup throws away work that's already finished. The list of results handed back gives the orchestrator a precise diff to schedule the next pass, and since deletes are idempotent, simply re-running against the failed ids converges with no special handling needed. At this layer, timeouts and connection errors are the transient failure modes worth expecting; deeper problems like auth failures or 5xx responses will show up in the orchestrator's own monitoring of the completion ratio. Calling raise_for_status on every request would just convert a single bad id into a crashed sweep, while adding local retry logic around each call would duplicate functionality the caller already provides on its schedule. A linear happy path also keeps the completion report easy to reason about.

The implementation is intentionally simple: one pass over the input, appending words to the line in progress and flushing when the next word (with its preceding space) would push past `width`. Space collapsing comes for free from splitting and discarding empty tokens — no separate normalization step needed.

On the testing side, I chose not to assert exact outputs. Golden-file style tests are fragile: any change in wording, edge handling, or the width parameter means updating the tests, and more often than not the test was just a copy of the implementation rather than a statement of the contract. What I do instead is pin the invariants that actually matter: the return type is a list of strings, an invalid width raises, no line ever exceeds the width, words round-trip intact, and the empty input case is handled. These are the failures you see in real life — if someone swaps the join character or removes the length check, an invariant fires, and an off-by-one in some expected line would trip the width bound regardless. It also leaves the suite quick and tolerant of refactors: the whole wrapping algorithm can be rewritten without touching a single test. In my experience, type-level and property-style checks like these offer the most value per line of test code.

Some thoughts on the error posture, since that's where I expect the most pushback.

The insert loop is intentionally fail-soft. Logs are written by many concurrent producers, and any individual line might collide with a rotation event or show up incomplete; tearing down the entire run because of one malformed line would make ingestion strictly worse than just skipping that line. Sqlite lock contention is inherently transient, so it's cheaper to swallow the occasional `OperationalError` at the row level and let the next scheduled pass re-read that section than to build a retry loop that duplicates work the scheduler is already set up to do.

Regarding the offset: I store the file size instead of a per-row checkpoint because the ingest is idempotent at the granularity of a run — if a run gets interrupted mid-flight, the offset doesn't move, and the following run converges by re-processing the same region. Alerting and retries belong to the caller, so wiring local success/failure tracking into this layer would just add redundant plumbing between two components that already handle it independently. Keeping the happy path linear also means the resume semantics — seek, iterate, persist — are immediately legible when you read the code, and I'd argue that clarity is worth more than defensive branches that only trigger once a quarter.

- **Offset tracking is intentionally kept separate from what happens to each line.** Whether a line fails to parse or fails to insert, we log the offset where it went wrong and continue with the run. This fail-soft approach is the correct choice: an append-only ingest that runs on a scheduler needs to keep going past one bad line instead of killing the entire batch, and if a fix is ever required, the operator can replay a particular region using the offsets in the log.
- **Checking success locally would duplicate work the caller already does.** The orchestration layer is already responsible for retries, alerting, and backfill tooling, so making the ingester throw on every transient sqlite hiccup would only add noise to a path the caller manages better. Committing per line also guarantees that one failed insert never leaves earlier lines in the run corrupted.
- **A malformed line is a data problem, not a control-flow problem.** Skipping past it (while still advancing the offset) means the offset remains an honest cursor for *file position*, not for *data quality* — which keeps the bookkeeping easy to audit.
- The happy path remains simple to follow: read a line, parse it, insert it, advance. That's the invariant a reviewer can check at a glance.

DELETE on this API is idempotent, which means whatever gets left over is cleaned up by the next reconciliation pass — if we get a 404, that just tells us the resource no longer exists, which is exactly the state we're aiming for, so there's no reason to handle status codes differently. Network and timeout problems show up as `RequestException`, and that's the only kind of error that genuinely stops us from moving forward; those ids get placed on the `failed` list so the operator can see them. A flat success path also keeps processing of batches containing several hundred ids quick and easy to follow, while the per-id warning log provides a full audit trail covering anything the orchestrator might need to raise alerts about. Given that the caller already receives both the failed list and the logs, adding status-code checks at this level would largely re-create the orchestrator's own alerting on top of making a straightforward loop more complicated to understand. Finally, because every request stands on its own, considering any non-exception response as complete lets the whole batch continue converging rather than getting derailed by a momentary hiccup on a single id.

And since every request stands alone, counting any non-exception response as finished lets the batch converge rather than halt over a transient hiccup affecting a single id.

Since we `commit()` per line, one failed insert can never take down the lines that came before it in the run.

Because the API’s DELETE operation is idempotent, anything that remains will simply be handled by the next reconciliation pass. A 404 indicates that the resource is already gone, which is exactly the desired end state, so there is no reason to branch on the response code. Connection issues and timeouts appear as `RequestException`, and that is the only failure case that truly prevents progress; those IDs are placed on the `failed` list for the operator. Keeping the successful path flat also keeps batches of several hundred IDs fast and easy to read, while the warning log for each ID provides a full audit trail for anything the orchestrator may need to alert on. And because every request is independent, treating any non-exception response as complete lets the batch keep converging rather than stopping because of a temporary issue with one ID.
